summary: DS-Lite reserved a small IPv4 block for a particular tunnel element. This document generalizes that reservation so it can also be used when an IPv6 transition solution needs to number a non-routed IPv4 interface.

eli5.summary: Some neighborhoods use house numbers that only make sense inside the neighborhood. This RFC reserves a small set of such private numbers for helper devices in networks moving from IPv4 to IPv6.

questions: what is the ipv4 service continuity prefix
how does 464xlat get an ipv4 address
subtitle: One small reserved IPv4 block, now shared by every IPv6 transition tool that needs a non-routed IPv4 address.

tldr.problem: DS-Lite reserved 192.0.0.0/29 for one element only, but other IPv6 transition systems such as 464XLAT also need a locally unique IPv4 address that never appears on the wire.
tldr.mechanism: IANA generalized the reservation so 192.0.0.0/29 is the IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix, usable by any system that needs IPv4 addresses for backward compatibility in an IPv6-only network.
tldr.outcome: One shared prefix serves DS-Lite and 464XLAT, with a rule that a host must not run two continuity solutions with overlapping 192.0.0.0/29 space.

today: RFC 7335 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6333. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Generalizing a DS-Lite Reservation
sections.content:
RFC 6333 (DS-Lite) told IANA to reserve 192.0.0.0/29 for the Basic Bridging BroadBand (B4) element. RFC 7335 widens that reservation to cover any case where a non-routed IPv4 interface must be numbered as part of an IPv6 transition solution.

The block is now called the IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix. It may be used in any system that needs IPv4 addresses for backward compatibility in an IPv6-only network but does not emit IPv4 packets on the wire. The change does not affect its use in DS-Lite.
sections.eli5: A club saved a few special seat numbers for one kind of guest. Now other kinds of guests can use those seat numbers too.

sections.title: The Case of 464XLAT
sections.content:
464XLAT (RFC 6877) provides IPv4 communication over an IPv6-only access network. In one of its methods the customer-side translator (CLAT) is embedded in a host such as a smartphone or a CPE (Customer Premises Equipment).

In that setup the host must have an IPv4 address configured so the host network stack and applications can bind IPv4 sockets. The address has to be locally unique to avoid conflicts with any other network that may talk to the CLAT.
sections.eli5: A phone that only speaks the new language still needs an old-style address to give to its apps, even if that address never leaves the phone.

sections.title: Choosing 192.0.0.0/29
sections.content:
In RFC 6333 this subnet exists only between the B4 and the Address Family Transition Router (AFTR) and never emits packets from this prefix on the wire. 464XLAT has the same need, and other similar solutions may too, so the RFC judges it most prudent to generalize the one prefix rather than reserve a new one for every possible solution.

There is one rule: a host MUST NOT enable two active IPv4 continuity solutions simultaneously in a way that would cause a node to have overlapping 192.0.0.0/29 address space.
sections.eli5: Everyone shares the same set of seat numbers, so one person must not use two helpers that both grab the same seats at once.

sections.title: IANA and Security Notes
sections.content:
IANA changed the IPv4 Special-Purpose Address Registry entry for 192.0.0.0/29 from "DS-Lite" (RFC 6333) to "IPv4 Service Continuity Prefix" (RFC 7335). The registry attributes include Source True, Destination True, Forwardable True, Global False and Reserved-by-Protocol False.

The RFC adds no security considerations beyond those in RFC 6333 and RFC 6877.
sections.eli5: The big list of special addresses now has a new label on this entry, and nothing new to worry about.
